issues.explanation: The cognitive formulation isolates Threat completely, so absence of Threat items is not itself a problem; however, the current profile strongly emphasizes trauma-memory reexperiencing and appraisals without any explicit threat content, making the night-specific avoidance item look weakly anchored to the rest of the selected profile.

issues.item: Avoid Night: Going out at night or being outside after dark
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Night' implies fear linked to darkness/outdoor danger, but there are no Threat items and no memory/trigger content tied to night-time, darkness, or outdoor contexts. For this relief-worker trauma, that strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is the least coherent item because it addresses a threat context not otherwise represented across Triggers, Memory, or Negative Appraisals.

issues.item: Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
issues.explanation: The formulation isolates Threat completely: all edges to and from Threat are inactive. Yet the selected Threat items are central, high-intensity PTSD threat responses and are also mirrored elsewhere. This makes Threat functionally active in a way that contradicts the formulation structure.

issues.item: Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
issues.explanation: Threat: Flashbacks and Threat: Physical Reactivity are tightly linked to the Memory and Triggers nodes, but the formulation specifies no active links involving Threat. Including these as Threat items makes the profile inconsistent with the stated node architecture.

issues.item: Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
issues.explanation: Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance and Maladaptive Strategies: Checking Surroundings both imply an ongoing current-danger/threat monitoring pattern, which again makes Threat clinically central despite Threat being fully disconnected in the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: Triggers: Entrapment: Having no options is the least coherent trigger relative to the rest of the profile. The remaining items focus on moral reminders and nightmare residue, while appraisals and strategies emphasize vigilance, rage, and fear of losing control. Entrapment could occur, but here it lacks a clear connection to the rest of the selected content and weakens coherence.

The cognitive formulation isolates Threat completely: all edges to and from Threat are inactive. However, the selected Threat items describe a prominent, connected threat response cluster (flashbacks, strong physical reactivity, concentration problems from reminders), which is difficult to reconcile with a formulation in which Threat has no active links to Triggers, Memory, Negative Appraisals, or Maladaptive Strategies.

Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance functions more like a current threat/safety-state belief and implies an active Threat system. That sits poorly with the formulation's fully inactive Threat node, especially when paired with checking surroundings and reactivity/flashback-type threat items.

The Threat node is clinically misaligned with the formulation: all incoming and outgoing Threat edges are inactive, so Threat should be relatively isolated or not central. However, the selected threat items describe an active symptomatic threat response cluster (strong emotional/physical reactivity and concentration disruption) that appears tightly tied to triggers and memory intrusions. This creates a contradiction with the formulation structure, especially given concurrent trigger and memory items that imply exactly the kind of reminder-linked threat activation the model marks as inactive. The other nodes are broadly coherent with each other and with the trauma type.

The Threat node is clinically incoherent with the provided cognitive formulation. Threat has no active incoming or outgoing edges, so it should not appear as a tightly integrated maintaining component. Yet all three selected Threat items are non-specific PTSD symptom/severity indicators rather than a coherent sense of current threat, and they are not meaningfully linked to the active Triggers, Memory, Negative Appraisals, and Maladaptive Strategies pattern.

Threat is structurally isolated in the formulation, but 'Scanning for Danger' is tightly mirrored by both Maladaptive Strategies: 'Checking Surroundings' and Negative Appraisals: 'I have to be on guard all the time,' making threat function as an active linked node rather than an isolated one.

Negative Appraisals: 'I have to be on guard all the time' overlaps almost exactly with Threat: 'Scanning for Danger' and Maladaptive Strategies: 'Checking Surroundings,' which contradicts the formulation because Threat has no active links to or from these nodes.

Threat: 'Negative Emotions' is very broad and non-specific, while the rest of the profile centers on intrusive reliving, moral/entrapment triggers, and vigilance-based coping; as a Threat item it does not fit the otherwise isolated, weakly integrated role of threat in this formulation.

vignette:
Mr. Anwar Rahman, an 80-year-old widowed South Eastern Asian man who had spent much of his working life as a data scientist, came to treatment describing a fear that had narrowed his world since his time as a relief worker in a war zone. He could still picture one night in particular: a crowded shelter with broken lights, shouting outside, families pressed into corners, and his team unable to move people to safety because armed men had blocked the only road out. The sense of having no options in that moment had stayed with him, and now even ordinary encounters could pull him back to it. If he saw people misbehaving in a store, arguing loudly on the street, or dismissing rules as if they did not apply to them, he felt the old alarm rise immediately. The same happened when he woke from a nightmare in a sweat, disoriented for a few seconds, still caught between sleep and the present. In those moments, Mr. Rahman would begin scanning the room, checking exits and windows, and mentally rehearsing what to say before speaking to anyone, as though careful preparation could keep the world from turning dangerous.

He described the memory itself as having an unnerving quality that made it impossible to place in the past. When he remembered the event, he did not experience it as something he had survived and left behind; he felt as if it was happening right now, like a film playing over and over with no break. The sounds, the pressure in his chest, and the feeling of being trapped returned with such force that his body reacted before he could reason with it. These memory surges were often followed by the same conclusion: if his reactions were this intense, perhaps he was going crazy. He had become frightened by his own anger as well, worrying that one day he would not be able to control it and would do something terrible. That fear of himself sat alongside a broader conviction that the world was dangerous, a place where violence and humiliation could erupt without warning. The more his mind returned to the war-zone scene, the more certain he became that danger was not over but waiting.

Over the months that followed, Mr. Rahman’s attempts to manage that dread made his symptoms more entrenched. He avoided news reports about events similar to what had happened to him, telling himself that he could not afford to let those images in. Yet when he did encounter a headline or a broadcast, even briefly, the familiar shelter scene flooded back with startling force, and his memories became vivid again, as if the old film had been started from the beginning. The same was true of encounters that echoed the original trap: a crowded hallway, a blocked doorway, or a situation where he felt there were no choices. Those moments were potent because they carried the same helplessness he had known in the war zone, and they immediately stirred the present-tense memory of being trapped. After one such episode in the lobby of his apartment building, he spent the rest of the day replaying the event in his mind and checking the surroundings every few minutes, trying to prevent a repeat. But the more he rehearsed and monitored, the more tightly the frightening scene seemed to cling to him, making the memory feel even less like something finished.

At work, where he still consulted part-time from home on data projects, Mr. Rahman found himself rehearsing conversations before every call and every meeting, worrying that a careless word or a sudden irritation would expose how unsettled he felt. He would spend long stretches scanning the environment around his desk, listening for raised voices in the building and watching the hallway through his door crack. Yet these efforts also kept the fear alive; each time he checked for danger, he was reminded that danger might be near, and each rehearsal confirmed how unsteady he believed himself to be. He came to the painful conclusion that his reactions meant he was losing his mind, and that belief deepened his anger and shame. A nightmare followed by waking in the dark would leave him tense and suspicious for the rest of the morning, and the next news bulletin or quarrel in the neighborhood would reopen the same memory. Over time he withdrew from social contact, spoke less with neighbors, and became increasingly isolated in his apartment, where the constant vigilance exhausted him.

By the time he sought help, Mr. Rahman was no longer only frightened by what had happened overseas; he was frightened by the way his mind kept bringing it back, by the anger he felt in his body, and by the possibility that he might become someone dangerous himself. What finally brought him in was his growing concern that the cycle was tightening around him: the nightmares, the scanning, the avoidance, and the replaying were leaving him more tense, more irritable, and more convinced that he could not trust either the world or his own reactions. He said he wanted relief, but what he feared most was that this would keep happening for the rest of his life and that he would end up alone, ruled by a danger that never truly stayed in the past.
